common_name: Oxford Blue Nigella (Deep Cobalt Blue Love-in-a-Mist)

planting.note: Direct-sow as soon as soil can be worked in spring, or in fall in mild climates; nigella has a fine taproot and resents transplanting.

directions: Oxford Blue bears semi-double, rich cobalt-blue flowers that read noticeably darker and more saturated than the soft powder-blue of the common species, set among the same thread-fine, feathery foliage. Scatter seed thinly and rake in lightly rather than sowing in rows, since love-in-a-mist looks most natural grown in loose informal drifts. Leave several stems unpicked so the inflated, veined seed pods can mature for dried-flower arrangements or for reliable self-seeding the following year. Deadhead spent blooms promptly if extending the bloom period is the goal, otherwise let pods form for late-season interest.

planting.note: Direct sow in fall in mild-winter climates for spring bloom, or in very early spring in colder regions; this old English heirloom does not transplant well and must be direct-sown into cool soil.

directions: Sybil Sherwood is a classic Victorian-era godetia selection prized for its salmon-pink petals edged in a fine picotee band of white, giving each satiny bloom a hand-painted, two-toned look. Sow directly into lean, well-drained soil, since rich ground pushes soft foliage growth at the expense of flowers and weakens stems. Grow in tight drifts rather than isolated plants, as the airy, upright stems support each other best in a mass planting. This is a cool-season crop through and through, so plan the display for late winter through spring and expect it to fade quickly once summer heat sets in.

planting.note: Direct sow in fall for winter establishment and spring bloom in mild climates, or in earliest spring in cold-winter regions; Clarkia amoena does not transplant well and needs cool soil to germinate evenly.

directions: Grace Salmon is part of the compact Grace strain of farewell-to-spring, bearing large, semi-double, satiny salmon-colored flowers with a subtly darker eye zone that reads warmer than the cooler-toned Grace Pink. Direct sow into lean to moderately fertile, well-drained soil and resist the urge to fertilize heavily, since excess nitrogen produces floppy growth and fewer blooms. Grow in generous drifts to show off the silky sheen of the petals, which catches light differently than the matte texture of most other cool-season annuals. Expect bloom from late winter into spring, tapering off once temperatures climb.

planting.note: Chill seed in the refrigerator for one to two weeks before sowing in earliest spring or fall to improve germination, since larkspur seed germinates poorly in warm soil.

directions: QIS Dark Blue is part of a uniform, well-branched larkspur series bred for commercial cut-flower production, producing tall spikes densely packed with fully double, deep violet-blue florets. Direct sow where plants are to bloom, since the brittle taproot rarely tolerates transplanting once established. Stake or net rows early, as the heavy flower spikes are prone to toppling in wind and rain once fully budded. Harvest when the lower third of each spike has opened for the best vase life, and expect bloom to finish quickly once summer heat arrives.

planting.note: Direct sow on the soil surface around the last frost, or in fall in mild-winter climates for winter and spring bloom; press seed in lightly since light aids germination.

directions: Northern Lights is a Moroccan toadflax strain selected for noticeably larger, more substantial snapdragon-like flowers than standard mixes, held on airy spikes above nearly invisible thread-fine foliage in a broad range of jewel-bright colors. Direct sow into well-drained, moderately fertile soil, since this cool-season annual declines fast once summer heat arrives. Mass plant in drifts along border edges or in rock gardens, where it self-sows readily in favorable conditions. Combine with poppies, larkspur, and other cool-season cutting-garden annuals for a layered spring display.

planting.note: Direct sow 2-4 weeks before last frost, or in fall in mild-winter climates; Cerinthe minor resents root disturbance and establishes best when sown in place.

directions: Kiwi Blue is a compact, bushier-growing honeywort than the taller Cerinthe major, bearing small tubular yellow flowers distinctly tipped in violet-blue and cupped by blue-flushed bracts, giving each cluster a two-toned jewel-like appearance. Direct sow into well-drained soil and avoid disturbing roots once seedlings emerge, since transplanting checks growth badly. The waxy, blue-gray foliage and nodding flower clusters are a magnet for bumblebees and look striking massed at the front of a cool-season border or trailing from a container. Allow some stems to set seed for reliable self-sowing in subsequent seasons.
